title: Tuning antibody stability and function by rational designs of framework mutations
source: Show notes link to https://doi.org/10.1080/19420862.2025.2532117; no further detail published in the episode notes.
one_line: The authors rationally designed mutations in antibody framework regions (outside the CDRs) to modulate stability and function, testing whether framework engineering can improve developability without redesigning the binding loops.
key_claims: Framework-region residues, not only CDRs, can be rationally mutated to tune antibody thermal/conformational stability.
Framework mutations are claimed to also affect function (binding/activity), implying the framework transmits effects to the paratope.
The approach is presented as a rational, generalisable design strategy rather than library-based screening.
No specific numerical values can be recorded from the published show notes, which contain only the DOI.
limitations: The episode's show notes contain only a DOI, so the specific antibodies, mutation sets, and quantitative stability/affinity changes cannot be verified here.
Rational framework design demonstrated on a limited panel of antibodies may not transfer across scaffolds, isotypes, or germlines.
Stability gains measured in vitro need not predict in vivo behaviour, aggregation in formulation, or immunogenicity risk from non-germline framework residues.
Effects on function are correlational unless structural evidence links framework changes to paratope conformation.
open_questions: Do the same framework mutations improve stability across a diverse, prospectively chosen antibody panel, or were they tuned per-antibody?
Do structures (crystal/cryo-EM) or MD show the mechanistic path from framework residue to CDR conformation?
Do the mutated frameworks raise immunogenicity risk given they deviate from germline sequence?
Do stability gains hold under manufacturing-relevant stress (freeze-thaw, high concentration, long-term storage)?
